transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
During a campaign stop in Nebraska, President Trump announced an executive order aimed at
lowering high diesel costs, dragging down Republicans ahead of the midterm elections.
The order eases limits on red dye diesel, which is identical to regular diesel but is
intended for off-road uses and exempt from some taxes.
In Nebraska, ranchers are also angry about Trump's plan to try to lower beef prices by
allowing in more imports.
Trump is campaigning for incumbent Republican Senator Pete Ricketts, who's facing an unexpectedly
competitive race with independent candidate Dan Osborne, who's backed by national Democrats.
President Trump says he will pay for the controversial TV ads that praise him, as NPR's Franco Ordonez
reports taxpayers have been footing the bill for the ads.
President Trump announced the new plan amid ongoing backlash over the publicly funded
spots running ahead of the midterms.
Trump defended the ads via his social media page, arguing that it was standard practice,
and that he was promoting the USA and "paying for them" with USA money.
But critics say the pro-Trump ads are blatantly partisan and use Republican talking points.
Trump says that he and his political action committee are taking over payment of the ads.
Franco, Ordonez, NPR News.
A major cryptocurrency spending group is backing 32 House candidates from both parties ahead
of the November midterms.
Fair shake will spend $1 million each to support six candidates, including several in competitive
races.
All 32 backed a major crypto bill that stalled in the Senate this year, in part because of
Democrats who said it was too lax on regulation.
Its largest investment is nearly $30 million against Ohio Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod
Brown, who's facing Republican John Husted.
Fair shake and its affiliates still have about $120 million available.
Schools across the country have long struggled to hire and keep teachers for areas like special
education, math and science, and Piazza Janakimeta reports most states aren't using higher pay
to help fill those jobs.
Extra pay is known to help attract and retain teachers, but the National Council on Teacher
Quality found 32 states offer no additional pay to draw and keep teachers in hard-to-fill
schools or subjects.
And the study says states are actually moving away from those kinds of incentives.
Only 13 states pay teachers extra for working in schools that have high turnover (that number
is down from 28 states in 2022), and only 17 states pay teachers more to work in hard-to-staff
subjects like math, science, or special ed (that's down from 22 states in 2022).
The report shows that high schools are struggling most at keeping teachers, especially those
serving families with low incomes.
All this comes as states face tighter budgets across the country.
Janakimeta, NPR News.
The U.S. stocks rose near their records today.
The S&P 500 added more than half a percent near its all-time high set over the summer.
This is NPR.
An American citizen shot by a federal agent a year ago during an immigration crackdown
in Chicago is suing the federal government.
She alleges the agent lied about the shooting and fired into her vehicle from behind.
Several prosecutors initially accused Marimar Martinez of using her vehicle to strike and
box in the agent's SUV in October 2025, but later dropped the charges.
Martinez was shot five times.
Russian authorities are playing down reports of an outbreak of the plague in Siberia.
NPR's Charles Maines reports a worker at a Siberian institute dedicated to the study
of the plague and other infectious diseases died of a mysterious illness.
Russia's consumer health watchdog, Ross Patreb-Nazur, said the victim was a 28-year-old female
lab worker at an anti-plague research facility in the Irkutsk region who had succumbed to
pneumonia of an unknown origin.
The local governor has since announced a state-run investigation found no pathogens in the lab
technician's body linked to her professional activities and pronounced the epidemiological
situation in the wider Irkutsk region stable.
Yet that statement was at odds with as-yet unconfirmed local media reports several hospitals
were under quarantine amid concerns over the spread of the mnemonic plague, a potentially
lethal airborne disease that was a focus of study at the Siberian lab.
Charles Maines, NPR News, Moscow.
Norway is proposing a temporary ban on AI glasses in certain public spaces.
The smart glasses can snap photos, record conversations or stream video without people
knowing.
The proposal reflects growing global concern about technology's changing daily life.
I'm Rylan Barton.
This is NPR News from Washington.

topics.text: President Trump announces executive order to lower diesel costs by easing red dye restrictions
Trump says he will pay for controversial TV ads praising him, not taxpayers
Cryptocurrency spending group Fair Shake backs 32 House candidates ahead of November midterms
Most states not using higher pay to attract teachers in hard-to-fill subjects and schools
U.S. stocks rise near record levels with S&P 500 gaining over half a percent
American citizen Marimar Martinez sues federal government over shooting by immigration agent in Chicago
Russian authorities downplay reports of plague outbreak at Siberian research facility in Irkutsk
Norway proposes temporary ban on AI glasses in certain public spaces over privacy concerns
